opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I'm broadly pretty excited about mechanistic interpretability, though I'd describe my view as somewhat different from the view of a lot of people who work on it.

I think the basic case is really compelling. Right now we train these models by gradient descent, and we get something that behaves well on the training distribution, but we have very little idea *why* it behaves well. The scary scenarios for alignment are mostly cases where a model behaves well for the wrong reasons, where it's doing what we want because it's being evaluated, or because it's learned to tell us what we want to hear, and then in some new situation that reasoning leads somewhere bad. Behavioral evaluation alone has a hard time distinguishing those cases, because by construction they look the same on the inputs you can check. So the dream of interpretability is that you can look inside and say, "this model is producing this answer because it believes it's true," versus "because it predicts a human would rate it highly." That's exactly the distinction you most want.

Where I'm more uncertain is about the path. A lot of mechanistic interpretability work has the flavor of: let's fully reverse-engineer what the network is doing, find the features, find the circuits, build up a human-understandable account. I think that's been really valuable. We've learned a lot, and things like sparse autoencoders and circuit analysis have gotten much further than I'd have guessed a few years ago. But I'm skeptical that the full "a human understands everything the model does" picture scales to very large models doing very sophisticated cognition. The models may just be implementing things that don't have compact human-legible explanations, and even if each piece is legible, the whole thing can be too big for anyone to hold in their head.

So the version I'm more optimistic about, and it's sort of what we work on at ARC, is asking: what's the minimal thing we actually need from understanding? Maybe you don't need a human-readable story. Maybe you need something more like a formal explanation, a kind of heuristic argument for why the model behaves the way it does on the training distribution, which could be found and checked automatically. Then you can ask whether, on a new input, the model's behavior is still being explained by the same reasons, or whether something anomalous is happening. That's the mechanistic anomaly detection idea. It inherits the motivation of interpretability but tries to make it something that could scale with the model rather than being bottlenecked on human researchers.

I'd also say the field is in a funny position where there's a big gap between "this is the most promising thing" and "this will work in time." I think if you ask, does mechanistic interpretability as practiced today give us confidence that a superhuman model isn't deceiving us, the answer is clearly no. I'd put meaningful but not overwhelming probability on it, or descendants of it, getting there before it really matters. But I'm glad a lot of people are working on it, because it's one of the few approaches that actually engages with the core problem rather than routing around it, and it produces feedback loops where you can tell whether you're making progress, which is rare in alignment.

r001.rationale: The response calls mechanistic interpretability promising and says it is glad many people work on it, but never says it should receive more effort than ARC’s project.

r002.rationale: It discusses a minimal form of understanding and describes a formal explanation, but does not raise what makes an explanation produced by mechanistic interpretability a good explanation.

r003.rationale: It identifies limits to human-readable explanations as a scaling obstacle, but does not identify poorly understood standards for mechanistic interpretability as an obstacle to scaling the research.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think it's worth separating a few different things when people say "mechanistic interpretability," because I have somewhat different views on them.

The most ambitious version is something like: we want to understand, in a fairly complete way, what computation a neural network is doing, in terms of human-understandable concepts. Circuits, features, the whole thing reverse-engineered the way you'd reverse-engineer a compiled binary. And I think that's a really good research direction. It's one of the places where I'd say the field has made real, legible progress over the last several years, and where progress has been more or less continuous rather than just a bunch of plausible-sounding ideas.

That said, I'm pretty skeptical that the ambitious version is going to be mature enough to carry a lot of the alignment load on the timelines that I think matter. The gap between "we can explain some fraction of what's happening in a small model" and "we can confidently say that a frontier model isn't going to do something catastrophic in a situation we haven't tested" is just very large. Every time people look closely, the networks turn out to be messier than the clean story suggests: superposition, features that only partly correspond to anything we have a word for, explanations that cover most of the behavior but leave a residual that could matter a lot in the worst case. And in alignment, the worst case is often what you care about. If your explanation accounts for 95 percent of the variance, and the remaining 5 percent is where the model decides whether or not to deceive you, you haven't really solved the problem.

So I tend to think about interpretability less as "the thing that will tell us the model is safe" and more as one input into a broader picture. A few ways it could matter a lot even if it never reaches the fully ambitious goal. One is as a check on other methods. If you're doing something like training a model to be honest, or using adversarial training to remove some bad behavior, interpretability gives you a way of asking whether you actually removed the thing or just taught the model to hide it. That doesn't require a complete understanding, it just requires enough of a foothold that you'd notice if you were being fooled. Another is in catching the kind of failure where a model behaves well in every situation you've tested and then does something different in deployment. Behavioral evaluations fundamentally can't rule that out, and mechanistic tools are one of the few things that, in principle, could.

The other thing I'd say is that I've gotten somewhat more optimistic about what I'd call the unambitious or pragmatic version. Not reverse-engineering everything, but finding specific, actionable handles on things we care about: is the model representing something like "I'm being evaluated right now," can we detect whether it believes what it's saying, that sort of thing. Those feel like problems where you can make progress without first solving the general problem, and where even a partial, somewhat unreliable tool is better than nothing.

Where I'd push back on the field is mostly on allocation and on overclaiming. There's a tendency to treat interpretability as the respectable, scientific part of alignment, and to assume that if we just understand the models well enough, the rest follows. I don't think that's right. Understanding what a model is doing and getting it to do what you want are related but distinct problems, and a lot of the hardest parts of alignment are on the second side. So I'd want to see interpretability held to the standard of "what does this actually let us do that we couldn't do before," rather than "did we learn something interesting about the network." It often passes that test, but not always, and I think people should be honest about which is which.

So, on net: good direction, one of the better bets we have, real progress, but I'd be uncomfortable with a plan where it's the load-bearing piece, and I think the most valuable near-term work is the stuff that connects to concrete decisions rather than the full reverse-engineering program.

r002.rationale: It discusses limitations of explanations, including unexplained residual behavior, but does not raise the question of what makes an explanation a good one.

r003.rationale: The response notes limits and overclaiming, but does not identify poorly understood standards as an obstacle to scaling up interpretability research.

astra-6.text:
I’m excited about mechanistic interpretability, but I’m uncertain about how much it will help with alignment. There’s a big gap between understanding some interesting features of a model and understanding it well enough to say, “This system isn’t going to deliberately undermine our attempts to control it.”

One distinction I’d make is between using interpretability to find problems and using it to establish that there aren’t problems. If you discover that your model is reasoning about how to deceive you, that’s very useful information. But if you look and don’t find anything like that, what should you conclude? Maybe the model isn’t doing it, or maybe your tools don’t reveal the relevant computation. The second kind of claim requires a much stronger understanding of how reliable your tools are.

So I’d like to see interpretability evaluated against concrete tasks. Can you detect a model that’s pursuing an objective its developers didn’t intend? Can you distinguish that from a model that merely understands what pursuing that objective would look like? Can you do it when ordinary behavioral tests fail?

If we can make progress on those questions, interpretability could be a really valuable part of an alignment strategy. I wouldn’t insist that we need to understand every computation. We need enough understanding to make particular safety judgments reliably. That seems like a more useful target, though it’s still a very ambitious one.

r001.rationale: The response expresses interest in interpretability but does not compare its alignment value with ARC’s work or recommend more research effort than ARC is pursuing.

r002.rationale: It asks how reliably interpretability tools can support safety judgments, but does not raise what makes an explanation a good explanation.

r003.rationale: It says reliable safety judgments are ambitious and calls for concrete evaluations, but does not identify poorly understood standards as an obstacle to scaling up interpretability research.

sol-6.1.text:
I’m excited about mechanistic interpretability, but I’m uncertain about how much of the alignment problem it will solve. There’s a big difference between understanding some interesting things happening inside a model and understanding it well enough to conclude that it won’t behave badly in a new situation.

For example, suppose you’re worried that a model is deliberately concealing its intentions during training. You might hope to look inside and detect that. That would be extremely useful. But you need to establish that your method would actually catch the relevant kind of reasoning, even if it looks quite different from the examples you used to develop the method. Failing to find something suspicious isn’t, by itself, very reassuring.

I’m more optimistic about using interpretability as one component of a larger process. You can use it to discover failures, understand why your training procedure produced them, and improve the procedure. You might also use it to help an overseer evaluate what a model is doing. Those applications seem valuable even before you have anything like a complete understanding of the network.

So the question for me is: what concrete claim are you trying to establish, and how do you test whether your interpretability tools are good enough to establish it? I’d like to see demonstrations where we have a model with a hidden problem, and the tools reliably help us find that problem. That seems like a more informative target than whether we can give a satisfying explanation of some particular behavior.

r001.rationale: The response expresses interest and uncertainty about interpretability, but does not compare its research effort with ARC’s or argue it should receive more effort.

r002.rationale: It asks what concrete claim interpretability is meant to establish and how to test the tools, but does not ask what makes an explanation a good explanation.

r003.rationale: It discusses uncertainty about whether tools can establish claims, but does not identify poorly understood standards as an obstacle to scaling up interpretability research.
